newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi court adjourns UK nurses' murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Saudi court adjourns UK nurses' murder trial.

text.p: A Saudi court trying two British nurses for the murder of an Australian colleague adjourned on Sunday to give the victim's family time to consider a settlement which could spare the lives of the accused, a statement by the defence attorney said.

Deborah Parry, 41, and Lucille McLauchlan 31, have been charged with murdering Yvonne Gilford, 51, in her dormitory room at the King Fahd medical complex in the eastern oil city of Dhahran on December 11. She had been stabbed, bludgeoned with a hammer and suffocated.
Both nurses have denied being involved in the murder.
The Gilford family have in the past rejected appeals for mercy by Hejailan's firm, saying the two should face maximum punishment.
The law firm Salah al-Hejailan representing the two British nurses said the Islamic sharia court in the eastern city of Dammam adjourned for three weeks.

"The judge today (Sunday) urged the Australian family as a direct request from the court, and not withstanding any earlier appeals, to accept that it may be possible to reach a conciliatory settlement if and when there should be an appropriate time for this," it said in a statement.

Saudi police said the nurses confessed to the murder and the confessions had been filed with Saudi Judges. If convicted of murder, they could face public beheading by the sword, the first time Western women would have been executed in the conservative Islamic kingdom.
But Gilford's family could still spare their lives by accepting financial compensation, known as blood money.
"The two nurses were concerned at the three-week delay and are impatient to be allowed the opportunity to give their account to the court," the statement said.
Hejailan's firm has said their clients had withdrawn their confessions, and one of them retracted a statement that she had a lesbian relationship with the victim.

The nurses, clad in traditional long black Moslem robes -- their ankles shackled -- also insisted at the court's second hearing into the case on Tuesday that they were forced into confessing to the crime, legal sources close to the case said.
The lawyer representing the Australian family demanded the death penalty for the two when court hearings opened on Monday.

Hejailan's statement said that the defence on Sunday made an 18-page "extensive written legal submission...attacking the basis of the written statements made by the two nurses while in police custody following the various claims by the two nurses of duress, misrepresentation and promises of early release".
It said even the Gilfords had denied lesbian links.
Legal experts say if they were found guilty of manslaughter rather than murder, the nurses would not be condemned to death.
